1. The animation shows how inflation erodes the buying power of a fixed income payment. It compares a "level" check, which stays the same, with a "rising" check, which increases over time. It uses an illustrative retiree, Carl, who starts in January 1966. In US history that was a stretch of fast price growth, about 6.38% a year. Buying power fell on all 20 of the 20 anniversaries.

2. Over time, prices rise and each crate of groceries costs more. Carl's first check buys 10 crates. By year 20 the same check buys only about 4 of 10 crates. In the last frames, the rising check is shown at 43.1% and the level check at 29.0%. These figures seem to be what each check still buys, as a share of the starting amount. In the final frame, the level check's bar is marked as "less than half".

3. It means a fixed payment loses a lot of real value over a long stretch of high inflation. A check that grows with prices keeps more of its value, but in this example it still falls well short of the original. The "Ruth" and "Carl" labels appear to contrast two cases. Ruth's check goes "back above" its starting level in the early years. Carl's "never" does. The frames are too small to tell exactly what separates them.

4. A viewer might take away that inflation matters for a long retirement, and that a payout that rises with prices (or has some inflation protection) holds its buying power better than a flat one. The animation doesn't tell anyone which option to pick. It also carries caveats: "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast".

5. The animation itself suggests the comparison: level vs rising checks, and buying power falling to under half. The advice to favor inflation protection is my own conclusion. The video, as shown, only presents the historical illustration and warns it isn't a forecast. A rising payout also usually starts lower, a cost the frames don't show.
